Empirical Research Plan:  Incidence and Welfare of Spatially Targeted Development Subsidies  

================================================================================
1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY  
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Preferred design:  “Fuzzy” geographic Regression-Discontinuity in combination with staggered Difference-in-Differences / event study.

Why?  
• Eligibility for most U.S. Enterprise / Empowerment Zones is rule–based: census tracts (or block-groups) must clear poverty or unemployment cut-offs taken from the most recent Decennial Census.  That creates a running variable (poverty rate or unemployment rate) and a sharp or fuzzy cutoff that can be exploited locally (RDD).  
• Actual subsidy intensity (dollars per worker, number of qualifying establishments, etc.) differs even among eligible tracts because states apply for and administer the programs.  Hence, use RDD‐based eligibility as an instrument for realized subsidy intensity within a DiD framework.  
• The staggered, multi-wave roll-out (1994, 1999, 2001, 2004 for federal EZ/EZ II/RC rounds; rolling adoptions of state zones) lets us estimate dynamic treatment paths, mobility responses, and spill-overs with modern two-way‐fixed-effects/event-study estimators (e.g. Sun & Abraham 2021 or Callaway & Sant’Anna 2021).

Design in one sentence  
1. Compare census tracts just above and just below statutory poverty/unemployment thresholds (“first stage”).  
2. Use that discontinuity as an instrument for total subsidy dollars received (“second stage”).  
3. Estimate effects on wages, employment, population, housing rents/prices, commuting flows in a staggered event-study.  
4. Interact treatment with ex-ante housing-supply elasticity (Saiz 2010) and mobility proxies to map equity-efficiency trade-offs.

================================================================================
2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL  
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
Ti,t  = log(1 + Subsidy_Dollars_Per_Worker) received by tract i in year t.  
Instrument: Eligibilityi (1 = tract poverty rate > 20 %, or unemployment > 1.5× metro rate in the designation year).

Control group  
• Tracts within a ±3 percentage-point bandwidth around the poverty/unemployment cutoff that are ineligible (Eligibility=0).  
• For DiD extensions we also use tracts in the same county that never become eligible as an additional control to sharpen power.

Treatment timing  
t0i = first year a tract’s designation becomes active (usually January after federal approval).  Event time k = t – t0i; k∈[–7,…,+10].

Running variable & cutoff (RDD)  
Running variable: Pi = tract poverty rate (1990 Census for first round, 2000 Census for later rounds).  
Cutoff: P̄ = 20 % (or unemployment Ui relative to metro).  Fuzzy because some >20 % tracts did not get selected and a few <20 % tracts slipped in through waiver provisions.

================================================================================
3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS  
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Local continuity: potential outcomes vary smoothly in tract poverty (or unemployment) in the absence of the program.  
Plausible? Reasonable within a narrow bandwidth; statutory cutoffs were not known far in advance, and poverty is hard to manipulate at the tract level.

A2. Monotonicity (IV): being above the cutoff weakly increases probability or intensity of subsidy receipt.  
Plausible? Yes—eligibility greatly raises selection probability; waivers are limited.

A3. Excludability (IV): the only channel through which eligibility affects outcomes is via subsidies.  
Plausible? Mostly; eligibility per se carries no direct funds, though publicity effects are minor.  We will show first-stage F-stats and test for discontinuities in pre-treatment covariates.

A4. Parallel trends for event-study: absent the program, near-cutoff treated and control tracts would have followed similar time trends.  
We will demonstrate with seven-year pre-period coefficients that they are statistically zero.

A5. Stable unit treatment / limited spill-overs within bandwidth.  
Spill-overs across tract boundaries are likely.  We include 5-km ring dummies, leave-one-county-out tests, and a spatial HAC variance estimator to gauge robustness.

================================================================================
4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATION  
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Threat 1. Manipulation of running variable (gerrymandered tract boundaries, data fudging).  
Check: McCrary density test; histograms.  If manipulation detected, shrink bandwidth or move to alternative running variable (pre-period unemployment).

Threat 2. Differential pre-trends or anticipation effects.  
Check: plot event-time coefficients k = –7,…,–1.  Insignificant estimates → passes.  Also, drop approval years to deal with anticipation.

Threat 3. General equilibrium spill-overs (jobs relocate from control to treated tracts).  
Approach:  
(a) Estimate net-of-spill-over effect at the county level (aggregate outcomes) as a bounding exercise.  
(b) Use Bartik-style shift-share instrument for national sector shocks to soak up common shocks.  
(c) Report separate “within tract” and “county residual” estimates.

================================================================================
5. R CODE OUTLINE  
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages ---------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)       # fast high-dim FE
library(rdrobust)     # RDD
library(modelsummary) # neat tables

# 1. Load data --------------------------------------------------------------
tract   <- fread("ez_tract_panel.csv")  # yearly tract outcomes 1985-2015
saiz    <- fread("saiz_supply_elasticity.csv") # housing elasticity by metro
tract   <- merge(tract, saiz, by = "cbsa", all.x = TRUE)

# 2. Construct key variables -----------------------------------------------
tract[, eligible  := as.integer(poverty_rate_1990 >= 0.20)]
tract[, post      := year >= ez_start_year]
tract[, subsidy_pc:= log1p(subsidy_dollars / employment)]
tract[, eventtime := year - ez_start_year]          # -7 … +10 ; NA if never treated
tract[, treat     := (eventtime >= 0)]
bandwidth <- 0.03
sample <- tract[abs(poverty_rate_1990 - 0.20) <= bandwidth]  # ±3pp window

# 3. First-stage (RDD) ------------------------------------------------------
rd_fs <- rdrobust(y = sample$subsidy_pc, x = sample$poverty_rate_1990 - 0.20,
                  fuzzy = sample$eligible)
summary(rd_fs)

# 4. 2SLS DiD Event-Study ---------------------------------------------------
# Sun & Abraham style: interact cohort × rel-time
sample[, cohort := ez_start_year]
# fixest will partial-out high-D FE
formula2sls <- subsidy_pc ~ 0 | treat*rel(eventtime) | 
               wages + rents + employment + population ~ eligible   |
               tract + year
# create demeaned event-time dummies excluding k = −1
for(k in -7:10){
  if(k != -1) sample[, paste0("D",k) := as.integer(eventtime == k)]
}

est <- feols(wage ~ (eligible) * i(eventtime, ref = -1) + 
             cbsa*time | tract + year,
             data = sample, cluster = "cbsa", iv = ~ eligible)
etable(est, title = "IV-Event Study: Wages")

# 5. Heterogeneity by housing elasticity -----------------------------------
est_het <- feols(wage ~ (eligible*high_elast) * i(eventtime, ref=-1) |
                 tract + year,
                 data = sample, cluster="cbsa", iv=~ eligible*high_elast)
etable(list(est, est_het),
       title = "Baseline vs. Heterogeneity by Housing Supply Elasticity")

# 6. Robustness: Alternate bandwidth (±5pp) -------------------------------
sample5 <- tract[abs(poverty_rate_1990 - 0.20) <= 0.05]
est_bw5 <- feols(wage ~ (eligible) * i(eventtime, ref=-1) |
                 tract + year,
                 data = sample5, cluster="cbsa", iv=~ eligible)
modelsummary(list("±3pp"=est, "±5pp"=est_bw5))
```

================================================================================
6. EXPECTED RESULTS  
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory suggests that with inelastic housing supply and mobile workers, the incidence of place-based subsidies falls mainly on landowners (higher rents) rather than incumbent workers.  In most distressed U.S. tracts, housing supply is relatively inelastic (median Saiz elasticity ≈1.5).  Therefore:  

• Rents: +2 – 4 % per $1,000 per worker in annual subsidy.  
• Wages of incumbent workers: small, maybe +0–1 %.  
• Employment / population: modest +1.5 % within tract, partly offset by –0.5 % in neighboring tracts.  
• Net county-level job gain: ≈+1 % (small but positive), implying some aggregate efficiency benefit if agglomeration spill-overs are present.  

================================================================================
7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT  
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
C1 (Local continuity around cutoff) ....................... 1  
C2 (Strong first-stage / relevance) ........................ 1  
C3 (No sorting/manipulation of running variable) .......... 0.5  
C4 (Parallel pre-trends / no anticipation) ................ 0.5  
C5 (Limited interference / SUTVA within chosen bandwidth) .. 0  

Total = 3 / 5.  The design is reasonable but vulnerable to spatial spill-overs and possible boundary manipulation; addressing these limitations is a key part of the empirical work.
